title: "Exploring personality hierarchies"
author: "Michael Hallquist"

```{r}
#| label: "setup"
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidyverse)
library(psych)
library(psychTools)
set.seed(12022024)
```

## Why "Bass-Ackwards"?

This short document walks through Goldberg's (2006) bass-ackwards approach for
visualizing personality hierarchies. Instead of assuming a top-down structure, we
start with a single-factor exploratory solution and keep increasing the number of
factors. By correlating factor scores from adjacent solutions we can observe how
higher-order traits differentiate into progressively narrower facets.

## Simulating a hierarchical Extraversion structure

We create 18 items designed to reflect two broad second-order themes of
Extraversion—Agentic Drive (assertive, driven, energetic) and Interpersonal
Vitality (warm, sociable, cheerful). Each of those breaks down into three facets,
and every facet has three items. All latent variables are standardized.

```{r}
#| label: "simulate"
n_people <- 1000
scale_vec <- function(x) as.numeric(scale(x))

orient_factors <- function(model) {
  load_mat <- unclass(model$loadings)
  signs <- sign(colSums(load_mat, na.rm = TRUE))
  signs[signs == 0] <- 1
  model$loadings[,] <- sweep(load_mat, 2, signs, `*`)
  if (!is.null(model$scores)) {
    model$scores <- sweep(model$scores, 2, signs, `*`)
  }
  if (!is.null(model$Phi)) {
    model$Phi <- model$Phi * outer(signs, signs)
  }
  model
}

# General Extraversion that feeds the second-order factors
extraversion <- scale_vec(rnorm(n_people))
agentic_noise <- rnorm(n_people)
interpersonal_noise <- rnorm(n_people)

agentic_drive <- scale_vec(0.7 * extraversion + sqrt(1 - 0.7^2) * agentic_noise)
interpersonal_vitality <- scale_vec(0.7 * extraversion + sqrt(1 - 0.7^2) * interpersonal_noise)

facet_specs <- tribble(
  ~facet,              ~second_order,            ~loading,
  "Assertiveness",     "Agentic Drive",          0.80,
  "Dominance",         "Agentic Drive",          0.75,
  "Activity",          "Agentic Drive",          0.70,
  "Sociability",       "Interpersonal Vitality", 0.80,
  "Warmth",            "Interpersonal Vitality", 0.75,
  "Positive Affect",   "Interpersonal Vitality", 0.70
)

make_facet <- function(parent, loading) {
  scale_vec(loading * parent + sqrt(1 - loading^2) * rnorm(n_people))
}

facet_scores <- facet_specs %>%
  mutate(parent = if_else(second_order == "Agentic Drive", "A", "I"),
         latent = map2(parent, loading, ~ if (.x == "A") {
           make_facet(agentic_drive, .y)
         } else {
           make_facet(interpersonal_vitality, .y)
         }))

item_loading <- 0.80
item_sd <- sqrt(1 - item_loading^2)

make_items <- function(latent, prefix) {
  map_dfc(1:3, ~ tibble(!!str_glue("{prefix}{.x}") := scale_vec(item_loading * latent + item_sd * rnorm(n_people))))
}

item_blocks <- facet_scores %>%
  mutate(prefix = str_c(str_sub(facet, 1, 3) %>% str_to_upper(), "_"),
         items = map2(latent, prefix, make_items))

item_data <- item_blocks$items %>% bind_cols()

item_data %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sd(.) %>% round(2))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "item", values_to = "sd") %>%
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

Even with random noise each item is standardized (SD ≈ 1), ensuring that factor
analysis is driven by latent structure rather than scale differences.

## Progressive exploratory factor analyses

We estimate principal-axis solutions from one through six factors, rotating with
Promax to allow correlations. The list below shows the salient loadings (>|.30|)
for the 1-factor solution and the 6-factor solution to highlight how the facets
emerge.

```{r}
#| label: "efa"
max_factors <- 6
efa_solutions <- map(1:max_factors, ~ fa(item_data, nfactors = .x, fm = "pa", rotate = "promax", scores = "regression"))
efa_solutions <- map(efa_solutions, orient_factors)

print_loadings <- function(model) {
  loadings <- fa.sort(model)$loadings
  #loadings[abs(loadings) < 0.30] <- NA
  print(loadings, cut=0.3)
}

cat("\n### 1-Factor solution\n")
print_loadings(efa_solutions[[1]])

cat("\n### 6-Factor solution\n")
print_loadings(efa_solutions[[6]])
```

Loadings and factor scores are re-oriented to keep the "high Extraversion" pole
positive in every solution, preventing arbitrary sign flips across levels. The
same reorientation is applied to the empirical analyses below.

With a single factor, every indicator reflects a common Extraversion dimension.
At six factors the items cleanly cluster back onto their generating facets,
providing a target to compare intermediate solutions.

## Tracking how factors split across levels

Bass-ackwards comparisons rely on correlating factor scores from consecutive
solutions. High correlations indicate lineage: a factor at level *k* "splits"
into whichever factors at level *k + 1* correlate most strongly with it. We call
the factors from the higher (smaller) solution "higher-order" because they
represent broader traits, whereas factors from the subsequent, more numerous
solution are "lower-order" facets.
We label each factor as `Lx_Fy`, where `Lx` denotes the level (number of
retained factors) and `Fy` indexes the rotated factors within that level, so
`L3_F2` is the second factor in the three-factor solution.

```{r}
#| label: "hierarchy"
score_list <- map2(efa_solutions, seq_along(efa_solutions), function(model, level) {
  scores <- as_tibble(model$scores)
  colnames(scores) <- str_glue("L{level}_F{seq_len(ncol(scores))}")
  scores
})

level_links <- map2_df(score_list[1:(max_factors - 1)], score_list[2:max_factors],
                      function(level_up, level_down) {
                        cm <- cor(level_up, level_down)
                        as_tibble(as.data.frame(as.table(cm))) %>%
                          rename(parent = Var1, child = Var2, r = Freq) %>%
                          mutate(level_from = str_extract(parent, "^L(\\d+)") %>% parse_number(),
                                 level_to   = str_extract(child,  "^L(\\d+)") %>% parse_number())
                      })

top_child_links <- level_links %>%
  group_by(child) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = abs(r), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(level_to, desc(abs(r)))

top_child_links %>%
  mutate(r = round(r, 2)) %>%
  select(level_from, parent, level_to, child, r) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Dominant correlations between adjacent solutions")
```

Most factors remain intact until the hierarchy reaches four or more dimensions,
at which point L1_F1 clearly differentiates into two children corresponding to
Agentic Drive (L2_F1) and Interpersonal Vitality (L2_F2). By the time we fit six
factors, those broad domains have further split into the six original facets with
adjacent correlations exceeding |.80|, mirroring the data-generating structure.

## Visualizing the lineage

The heatmap below offers another way to scan how each level connects to the next
by showing all correlations rather than only the dominant ones. Each rectangle depicts how higher-order factors (i.e., from a solution with fewer factors) divide into lower-order factors when we increase the number of factors by one.

For example, lower left rectangle shows how a one-factor solution for extraversion (L1_F1 on the x axis) divides into two factors (L2_F1 and L2_F2) on the y axis. Likewise, the upper right rectangle shows how a five-factor solution (on the rows, spanning L5_F1 -- L5_F5) maps onto a six-factor solution (columns L6_F1 -- L6_F6).

```{r}
#| label: "heatmap"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| message: false
link_heatmap <- level_links %>%
  mutate(pair = str_c(parent, " → ", child))

ggplot(link_heatmap, aes(x = parent, y = child, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "BrBG", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Higher-order factor", y = "Lower-order factor",
       fill = "r",
       title = "Bass-Ackwards correlations across adjacent solutions") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

For example, the first column (`L1_F1`) shows uniformly strong tiles with both
`L2_F1` and `L2_F2`, illustrating how the single higher-order Extraversion factor
splits into the Agentic versus Interpersonal lower-order dimensions at level 2.
By level 3 you can see `L2_F1` tying most strongly to `L3_F1` and `L3_F2`, which
correspond to Dominance and Activity facets, while `L2_F2` links to `L3_F3` to
recover Sociability. Reading down any column reveals the sequence of facets that
inherit variance from that broader ancestor.

For the upper right rectangle (5 vs. 6), we primarily see that L5_F1 (the first factor from
the five-factor solution) splits into L6_F3 and L6_F6, while most of the other have a nearly 1:1 correspondence (e.g., L5_F2 [x axis] maps to L6_F1 [y axis] pretty cleanly).

## Takeaways

1. **Begin with the broadest structure.** The single-factor solution captures the
   highest-order Extraversion trait that underlies all items.
2. **Increase the dimensionality stepwise.** Moving to two and three factors
   reveals the first splits (Agentic vs. Interpersonal emphases) before facets
   emerge.
3. **Use correlations as breadcrumbs.** By correlating factor scores across
   levels, we can label lower-order traits according to the higher-order factor
   they most closely align with, effectively "growing" the hierarchy from the
   top down.
4. **Cross-check with theory.** The simulated data intentionally mirrors accepted
   Extraversion facets, but with real data this workflow provides a transparent
   way to test whether empirical splits reproduce theoretical expectations.

## Empirical validation with the BFI

The `psychTools::bfi` data contain 2,800 participants who answered 25 Big Five
items (five per domain). After listwise deletion across those items we retain
2,436 respondents, reverse-key the negatively worded indicators, and standardize
each column so the empirical example parallels the simulated workflow.

```{r}
#| label: "bfi-prep"
data("bfi", package = "psychTools")
data("bfi.dictionary", package = "psychTools")

bfi_dict <- bfi.dictionary %>%
  rownames_to_column("code") %>%
  select(code, Big6, Little12, Item, Keying)

bfi_items_raw <- bfi %>%
  select(matches("^[A-Z][1-5]$")) %>%
  drop_na()

reverse_items <- bfi_dict %>%
  filter(code %in% names(bfi_items_raw), Keying == -1) %>%
  pull(code)

bfi_items <- bfi_items_raw %>%
  mutate(across(any_of(reverse_items), ~ 7 - .)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), scale_vec))

tibble(n_people = nrow(bfi_items), n_items = ncol(bfi_items))
```

### Mapping items to theoretical facets

To interpret empirical splits we pair each item with its domain and facet labels,
and flag the reverse-keyed prompts, using `bfi.dictionary`. The `Big6` column in
that dictionary names the higher-order domain in Goldberg's "Big Six" taxonomy,
which mirrors the Big Five domains (Agreeableness, Conscientiousness,
Extraversion, Openness) but replaces Neuroticism with its positive pole,
Emotional Stability, and optionally adds an Honesty-Humility domain not covered
by the BFI. The `Little12` column lists the narrower facet (e.g., Compassion vs.
Politeness within Agreeableness). The Extraversion items mainly tap
Assertiveness versus Sociability facets (Little12 labels), giving us a
theoretical benchmark for the empirical bass-ackwards splits.

```{r}
#| label: "bfi-dictionary"
bfi_dict %>%
  select(code, Big6, Little12, Item) %>%
  filter(str_detect(code, "^E[1-5]$")) %>%
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Item", "Big Six", "Facet (Little12)", "Prompt"),
               caption = "BFI Extraversion items and their theoretical facets")
```

```{r}
#| label: "factor-label-helper"
derive_factor_labels <- function(models, dict, threshold = 0.30) {
  label_list <- map2(models, seq_along(models), function(model, level) {
    load_tbl <- unclass(model$loadings) %>%
      as_tibble(rownames = "code") %>%
      pivot_longer(-code, names_to = "factor_raw", values_to = "loading") %>%
      filter(!is.na(loading), abs(loading) >= threshold) %>%
      left_join(dict, by = "code") %>%
      mutate(level = level,
             factor_num = parse_number(factor_raw))

    if (nrow(load_tbl) == 0) {
      return(tibble())
    }

    load_tbl %>%
      group_by(level, factor_num) %>%
      summarise(
        domain = {
          vals <- Big6[!is.na(Big6)]
          if (length(vals) == 0) "Mixed" else names(sort(table(vals), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
        },
        facet = {
          vals <- Little12[!is.na(Little12)]
          if (length(vals) == 0) "Mixed" else names(sort(table(vals), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
        },
        .groups = "drop"
      ) %>%
      mutate(
        factor_id = str_glue("L{level}_F{factor_num}"),
        label = str_glue("{factor_id}: {domain} ({facet})")
      ) %>%
      select(level, factor_num, factor_id, domain, facet, label)
  })

  list_rbind(label_list)
}
```

### Bass-ackwards splits for Extraversion items

The five Extraversion indicators primarily reflect a single factor but begin to
differentiate into sociability versus assertiveness emphases once we allow a
second dimension. Even with only five items the bass-ackwards logic clarifies
how the general Extraversion factor fragments.

```{r}
#| label: "bfi-extraversion"
bfi_extraversion <- bfi_items %>% select(matches("^E[1-5]$"))

ext_max_factors <- 2
ext_solutions <- map(1:ext_max_factors,
                     ~ fa(bfi_extraversion, nfactors = .x, fm = "pa",
                          rotate = "promax", scores = "regression"))
ext_solutions <- map(ext_solutions, orient_factors)

cat("\n### BFI Extraversion: 1-factor\n")
print_loadings(ext_solutions[[1]])

cat("\n### BFI Extraversion: 2-factor\n")
print_loadings(ext_solutions[[2]])

ext_scores <- map2(ext_solutions, seq_along(ext_solutions), function(model, level) {
  scores <- as_tibble(model$scores)
  colnames(scores) <- str_glue("L{level}_F{seq_len(ncol(scores))}")
  scores
})

ext_links <- map2_df(ext_scores[1:(ext_max_factors - 1)], ext_scores[2:ext_max_factors],
                     function(level_up, level_down) {
                       cm <- cor(level_up, level_down)
                       as_tibble(as.data.frame(as.table(cm))) %>%
                         rename(parent = Var1, child = Var2, r = Freq)
                     })

ext_links %>%
  mutate(r = round(r, 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "BFI Extraversion: correlations between adjacent solutions")
```

The two-factor solution separates sociability-focused prompts (E1, E2, E4; all
Little12 = Sociability) from assertiveness prompts (E3, E5; Little12 =
Assertiveness). E4's positive sociability loading anchors
the "talkative/friendly" pole, whereas E3 and E5 define the "leadership/forceful"
pole. The pattern mirrors the dictionary facets, showing how the hierarchy
recovers theorized nuances even within five observed indicators. Because the
items were reverse-keyed before standardization, higher factor scores now always
reflect more of the named trait.

### Building the full Big Five hierarchy

Next we apply the same workflow to all 25 items. We end the sequence at six
factors so the model can first recover the overall Big Five structure before
hinting at narrower groupings.

```{r}
#| label: "bfi-big5"
big5_max_factors <- 6
big5_solutions <- map(1:big5_max_factors,
                      ~ fa(bfi_items, nfactors = .x, fm = "pa",
                           rotate = "promax", scores = "regression"))
big5_solutions <- map(big5_solutions, orient_factors)

big5_factor_labels <- derive_factor_labels(big5_solutions, bfi_dict)
```

The helper summarizes each factor's dominant `Big6` domain and `Little12` facet
based on the items that load on it. Those labels accompany the lineage table and
heatmap below so readers can directly connect the empirical factors to their
theoretical Big Six / Little Twelve interpretations. Because the BFI lacks an
Honesty-Humility scale, the `Big6` labels for the 5-factor solution align exactly
with the traditional Big Five domains (with Neuroticism shown as Emotional
Stability); when we expand to six factors the labels still reference the same
domains but the `Little12` facets signal which subcomponent (e.g., Orderliness
vs. Industriousness) has split off.

```{r}
#| label: "bfi-big5-loadings"

cat("\n### BFI items: 1-factor solution\n")
print_loadings(big5_solutions[[1]])

cat("\n### BFI items: 5-factor solution\n")
print_loadings(big5_solutions[[5]])

cat("\n### BFI items: 6-factor solution\n")
print_loadings(big5_solutions[[6]])

big5_scores <- map2(big5_solutions, seq_along(big5_solutions), function(model, level) {
  scores <- as_tibble(model$scores)
  colnames(scores) <- str_glue("L{level}_F{seq_len(ncol(scores))}")
  scores
})

big5_links <- map2_df(big5_scores[1:(big5_max_factors - 1)], big5_scores[2:big5_max_factors],
                      function(level_up, level_down) {
                        cm <- cor(level_up, level_down)
                        as_tibble(as.data.frame(as.table(cm))) %>%
                          rename(parent = Var1, child = Var2, r = Freq) %>%
                          mutate(level_from = str_extract(parent, "^L(\\d+)") %>% parse_number(),
                                 level_to   = str_extract(child,  "^L(\\d+)") %>% parse_number()) %>%
                          mutate(parent = as.character(parent),
                                 child = as.character(child))
                      })

big5_top <- big5_links %>%
  group_by(child) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = abs(r), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(level_to, desc(abs(r)))

big5_top_labeled <- big5_top %>%
  left_join(big5_factor_labels %>%
              select(parent = factor_id, parent_domain = domain, parent_facet = facet),
            by = "parent") %>%
  left_join(big5_factor_labels %>%
              select(child = factor_id, child_domain = domain, child_facet = facet),
            by = "child")

big5_top_labeled %>%
  mutate(r = round(r, 2)) %>%
  select(level_from, parent, parent_domain, parent_facet,
         level_to, child, child_domain, child_facet, r) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Dominant BFI correlations between adjacent solutions")
```

The lineage table shows the classic path: a single general factor (sometimes
interpreted as the "General Factor of Personality") splits into the Big Five by
the time five factors are retained. Moving to six factors introduces subtle
shifts: the Conscientiousness branch stays anchored on Orderliness indicators
(C1–C3) while the more work-ethic items (C4–C5) begin to share variance with an
additional, weaker factor, and the Openness branch splits its Intellect-labeled
items into two closely related clusters (idea-rich O1–O3 versus reflective O4–O5
content). Because the BFI Agreeableness scale contains only Compassion prompts,
no distinct Politeness node emerges in this dataset. The dictionary labels
provide a quick bridge from the empirical splits back to the facets actually
represented in the items.

```{r}
#| label: "bfi-heatmap"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| message: false
label_lookup <- setNames(big5_factor_labels$label, big5_factor_labels$factor_id)
lookup_or_id <- function(ids) {
  labs <- label_lookup[ids]
  labs[is.na(labs)] <- ids[is.na(labs)]
  labs
}

ggplot(big5_links, aes(x = parent, y = child, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "BrBG", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = lookup_or_id) +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = lookup_or_id) +
  labs(x = "Higher-order factor (with Big Six / Little12 labels)",
       y = "Lower-order factor (with Big Six / Little12 labels)",
       fill = "r",
       title = "BFI bass-ackwards correlations across adjacent solutions") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

Axis labels now display the dominant Big Six domain and Little12 facet inferred
from the dictionary lookups, so each tile immediately conveys both the lineage
and its likely substantive interpretation (e.g., `L5_F4: Openness (Intellect)`
linking strongly to both `L6_F4: Openness (Intellect)` and `L6_F6: Openness
(Intellect)`, signaling that the Intellect-focused prompts have begun to split
into two subclusters).

### Empirical takeaways

- The observed Extraversion indicators mirror the simulated hierarchy: a single
  dominant factor that splits into sociability and assertiveness nuances when the
  dimensionality increases.
- Running all 25 BFI items through the bass-ackwards routine recovers the Big
  Five domains at five factors and reveals plausible sub-facets when adding a
  sixth factor, demonstrating how empirical data follow the same lineage logic as
  the simulated example.
